title: The Second Turn in Philosophy: From Consciousness to Language
summary: Philosophical history does not proceed in a straight line. The basic nature of the world in any age becomes the principal question; the possibility of knowledge in another age; then the consciousness, self-awareness and feeling of the knower; And in many influential currents of the twentieth century, language, meaning, signs, usage, logical forms, rules and communication become the focus of philosophical inquiry. This change is often referred to as the “linguistic turn”. But the linguistic turn did not mean that philosophy left the world, mind, morality, history or society and began to see only the meaning of words. The basic problem is more serious: humans understand the world through language, concepts, classifications, sentences, logic and shared rules; So how can the question of knowledge and reality remain completely separate from language? An influential line of European modern philosophy begins with the consciousness of the knower. Descartes' methodological skepticism seeks the certainty of the knower by examining the external world, the senses, tradition, and the basis of belief. Locke examines the sources of experience, Berkeley the relationship between perception and object-existence, Hume the self, causality and arrival, and Kant the potential conditions of perception. In this tradition, the question is simply “What is the world?” No living, but rather “how does the world appear in my experience?”. is formed. With this achievement, a limitation is also evident: if the knower is assumed to be a stand-alone consciousness, then the role of language, social training, shared rules, public meanings and counterarguments is obscured. Here is the crux of the chapter's problem: how to understand the transition from consciousness-centered modern philosophy to language-centered twentieth-century philosophy without the fallacy that language completely supplants reality? Furthermore, how can Indian philosophy—especially Nyaya, Mimansa, Grammar, Buddhist Pramanamimansa—and the Navya-nyaya of Mithila be included in this discussion without the triumphal claim that “the Indian tradition had already said all the modern theories”? The basic assertion of this chapter is that the linguistic turn of the twentieth century is not a negation of consciousness-centered philosophy, but an extension of it. The knower is not only the private mind; He is also a linguistic, social, historical and rule-driven creature. Humans share meanings, learn definitions, improve the use of signs, present arguments, accept oppositions, and make decisions in institutionalized language. Therefore Knowledge, truth, metaphysics, ethics, politics and history—all are influenced by language. But the other half of this assertion is equally essential: language is not omnipotent. The physical phenomenon of an earthquake is not dependent on the word “earthquake”; The biological process of disease does not end with the name of diagnosis; The river would not change its water course by changing the category on paper; Historical events would not become uneventful by being suppressed in the records. Language, therefore, collides with objective resistance even as it participates in the construction of social reality. Parallel philosophy rejects two extremes for this reason. First—language is only a transparent glass, which has no active effect on knowledge. Second—all reality is constructed by language, so the question of truth outside language is meaningless. Between these two is the assertion: language is the active medium of human experience, classification, communication and interpretation of reality; But language is not the only criterion for truth. Proof, argument, objective resistance, counterargument and re-examination are necessary.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 1 · English translation
purvapaksha: The former might suggest that the linguistic turn takes philosophy away from the real question. The basic questions of philosophy are God, the soul, the world, freedom, justice, death, society and suffering; Analysis of words, sentences and usage cannot replace this problem. If there is hunger in society, looking at the grammar of the word “hunger” will not provide food; If there is injustice, saying language-game will not change the institution. Therefore, linguistic philosophy risks turning philosophical problems into academic wordplay. The second variant of the former view is that increasing the importance of public usage will make truth dependent on majority or prevalence. If meaning is in use, should what society says be true? Social norms can be wrong, discriminatory or oppressive. Language itself can carry biases. Therefore, publicity is not a sufficient criterion of truth. The third premise applies to comparative philosophy. The Indian tradition has long discussed words, sentences, proofs and meanings; In such a situation, it may be West-centric history that gives particular novelty to the modern linguistic turn. The hyperbole of the reverse side might say that whatever Frege, What Russell or Wittgenstein said, what Nyaya, Mimansa, Bhartrihari or Navya-nyaya had already said.
uttarapaksha: The answer to the first premise is that language is the entrance, not the final destination, of philosophy. To remove injustice, policies, institutions, resources and power must change; But the policy debate itself can become confusing when the meaning of concepts like “rights,” “equality,” “disadvantage,” “person,” “community,” “race,” “religion,” and “freedom” are unclear. Laws are made in language, evidence is presented in language, orders are issued in language, oaths and affirmations are linguistic acts. So language is not the external decoration of real life. The answer to the second premise is that usage is a source of meaning, not the ultimate proof of truth. Society makes the wrong rules; The majority can accept misclassification; Institutional language can be oppressive. Therefore, while acknowledging the sociality of meaning, evidence, reasoning, moral criticism and objective resistance remain necessary. “What is in vogue” and “what is true or proper” are not the same thing. The answer to the third precedent is in the comparative method. The antiquity of the linguistic discourse of the Indian tradition must be acknowledged, but also the historical independence. Navya-nyaya = not analytical philosophy; Bhartrihari = not structuralist; Apoh = not deconstruction; Polytheism = not postmodern relativism. The presence of similar questions does not prove historical identity. The real intellectual benefit comes when the arguments of different traditions are pitted against each other and examined. The general formula for parallel answers is: make the statement clear; understand its linguistic structure; Then ask—what reality does he claim, what is the evidence for it, what are the social consequences, what are the moral justifications, what are the counterarguments, and whether the conclusion will change when new evidence comes along. Language is the gateway; The world, experience, institutions, power and morality are the next areas of the journey.
synthesis: The linguistic turn of the twentieth century would not have eliminated the consciousness-centered questions of modern philosophy; It opens up its social, logical and linguistic dimensions. The knower is not speechless consciousness. They learn language, obey rules, correct expressions, listen to counterarguments, and share meaning in the social world. For this reason, truth, knowledge, metaphysics, ethics, politics and history cannot be completely separated from language. But to focus on language is not to merge the world into language. The formula of parallel philosophy is: language is the active medium of human experience of reality; not the sole creator of truth. Language can classify and shape social reality, but bodies, matter, pain, nature, history and evidence resist its limits. Indian jurisprudence, mysticism, grammar and Buddhist linguistic discussion are independent traditions, not historical precursors of modern linguistic philosophy. The Navya-nyaya of Mithila is not an analytic philosophy either; But the linguistic clarity, the subtlety of relationships, the discipline of proof, absence, inference and counterargument open up a fruitful dialogue with modern questions. Five formulas emerge from this chapter. First—consciousness is an important focus of philosophical questions, but not the only one. Second—language is not merely the outer covering of thought; is the active medium of conceptual knowledge. Third—meaning is not merely a private feeling; It is associated with usage, rules, context and shared behaviour. Fourth—language can shape social reality, but reality is not language alone. Fifth, the comparison of Indian and modern Western linguistic traditions should be for problem-solving, not to prove historical similarities.

title: Why Philosophy Changed in the Twentieth Century
summary: The names of philosophers and the order of their works alone are not enough to understand twentieth-century philosophy. The question is, what changed so that many philosophical beliefs that were current until the end of the nineteenth century became the subject of re-examination in the twentieth century? Science became more consolidated as an independent institutional discipline; New geometry and set-theory were questioned in mathematics; Symbolic reasoning changed the boundaries of the old mode of reasoning; In physics, the theory of relativity forced a rethinking of ordinary notions of space, time, and measure; Psychoanalysis questioned the transparency of self-perception; Linguistics opened the way to view language as a system of relations, not a list of names; The World War shocked the confidence of modern progress and sanity; Colonial rule and resistance created a situation to re-examine the language of sovereignty, civility, nation, rights and history; And the modern state administration, census, law, education, records, police, military, health and statistics began to classify human life in an unprecedented way. Not all of these changes occurred for the same reasons, nor did all philosophers give the same answers. The history of twentieth-century philosophy cannot be summed up in a simple formula. However, there appears to be a common position: philosophy had to re-clarify its subjects, methods and justifications. As physics, biology, psychology, sociology, and mathematics formed their own distinct methodological and institutional fields, the question arose—what is philosophy’s own job? Does philosophy offer any particular knowledge above experience, analyze concepts of science, clear up linguistic confusion, search for the meaning of human-existence, critique power and society, or a different combination of these functions? The problem of this chapter is not to find the causes of these changes, but to understand the transformation of the problem-domain. An event in history “produced” a theory of philosophy—such mechanical causality is unacceptable. More appropriately, science, mathematics, language, psychology, war, colonialism, and new forms of state provided new pressures, new evidence, new languages, and new crises to philosophical questions. The basic assertion of this chapter is that the transformation of twentieth-century philosophy is not merely a coincidence of seven or eight distinct currents, but rather the authority of knowledge, the nature of reason, . It was a simultaneous re-examination of the transparency of the self, the role of language, the direction of history, the power of the state and claims to universality. Old questions did not disappear; His terms changed. There were already questions about God, soul, truth, causality, freedom, justice, knowledge, language and society, but in the twentieth century new science, new reason, new institutions and new political experiences changed their way of asking. Science challenged philosophy from two directions. First, science began to answer questions by its own evidence and methods that had previously been under natural philosophy. Second, revolutions within science challenged philosophical beliefs themselves. Non-Euclidean geometry and the theory of relativity presented a picture of space that differed from ordinary experience and some philosophical presuppositions. Consequently, the meaning of terms like “inevitable”, “precedential”, “natural”, and “self-evident” was re-examined. Mathematical logic changed the language of philosophical reasoning. The work of Frege, Russell, Whitehead, and later logicians showed that general grammar and logical structure are not the same thing. quantities, relations, prohibitions, existences, functions and inferences more formally can be expressed. These changes produced new ideals of clarity, formalism, and analysis in philosophy, although even the limits of these ideals were later severely criticized.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 2 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first premise might say that “philosophy changed in the twentieth century” is itself an exaggerated sentence. The philosophy was always changing; From Plato to Aristotle, from Buddhism to neo-judgment, from the Middle Ages to modernity—everywhere there were serious changes. It may therefore be a self-glorification of European modernity to regard the twentieth century as a special turning point. The second premise is that deducing philosophy from the changes of science poses a crisis of scientism. Einstein's theory is successful physics, but it does not automatically solve questions of morality, religion or meaning. Gödel’s theorem is a typical result of formal mathematics; It is inappropriate to make it a general slogan like “the human mind is always above the machine”. Because of Freud's historical influence, not all of his psychological claims could be considered true. The third precedent applies to political history. War, colonialism, or crises of state power affect philosophical thought, but the independent value of reason can be destroyed if thought is considered “determined” only by social circumstances. A philosophy was written in wartime—that is why it is not true or false. Fourth former Indian is from the point of view. If the changes of the twentieth century are based on science, Frege, Freud, Saussure, World War II and European imperialism, then Indian tradition will become merely a reaction to Europe. Indian philosophy's long debates on its proof-metaphysics, logic, language, soul, emptiness, karma, religion, society and liberation may be marginalized in this map. The fifth precedent is in the context of Mithila. It would be an injustice of history to measure a highly developed logical tradition like the Neo-Nyaya by the standards of modern symbolic logic. The question of the Tattvachintaman and its commentary tradition is different from the question of modern mathematical logic. Therefore, the “modernity came, the old philosophy became irrelevant” conclusion is unacceptable.
uttarapaksha: The answer to the first premise is that the twentieth century is being described as a period of specific problem-combinations, not a “unique” or “greatest” turning point. Philosophy changed in the post-eastern period; The twentieth century is characterized by the fact that the institutional autonomy of science, mathematical logic, the industrial war, the people state, the colonial crisis, mass communication, psychology and linguistics exert concomitant philosophical pressures in a historical horizon. The answer to the second precedent—parallel philosophy scientism rejects. The results of science have high evidential-value in areas where scientific methods are applicable; But moral justification, political legitimacy, meaning, dignity or religious claims demand a different kind of logic and evidence. Respect for science should be accompanied by an understanding of the limits of science. For this reason, “Science proved, therefore philosophy is over” and “Philosophy is independent, therefore science is irrelevant”—both extremes are unacceptable. Answer to the third premise—the historical context does not replace the philosophical argument, but clarifies its question-status. War experience would not prove “conscience is bad”; He gives reason to ask that instrumental efficiency and why moral conscience is not the same thing. Colonialism would not prove “universalism false”; He shows that universal claims can have selective application in practice, so the criterion should be more stringent. Answer to the fourth premise—It is wrong to regard Indian philosophy as a response to modern European phenomena. Questions of Indian tradition are historically independent. However, the colonial and postcolonial conditions of the twentieth century changed the study, teaching, translation, classification and public meaning of these traditions. The independent tradition dialogues with the modern context; Dialogue does not mean origin. Answer to the fifth preliminary argument—The Navya-nyaya of Mithila need not be proved to be equivalent to or a precursor to modern logic. The real question is what questions a very subtle proof-logic tradition poses to modern science, linguistics, formal logic and university philosophy. Comparing the two traditions while preserving historical differences makes the boundaries of the two traditions more apparent.
synthesis: Philosophy did not change in the twentieth century because a single philosopher discovered a new method. The change was profound, as the whole landscape of knowledge changed. Science became an institutional force separate from philosophy; Revolutions within science challenged old certainties; Mathematical reasoning changed the formal form of thought; Psychoanalysis questioned the transparency of the self; Linguistics saw meaning in mechanisms of structure and differentiation; The World War broke moral assurances of progress; Colonialism exposed the selective use of universalism; The modern state intensified knowledge-power relations through classification, records and administration. It is not appropriate to melt these into one theory. Logical directivism, phenomenalism, existentialism, structuralism, critical theory, postcolonial thought and later poststructuralism have different questions, methods and answers. The philosophical characteristic of the twentieth century is not consensus, but expansion of the problem-field. From an Indian point of view, this change means neither Western imitation nor a repetition of ancient glory. Nyaya, Mimansa, Grammar, Buddhism, Jainism, Vedanta and other traditions have independent intellectual histories; Modern science, colonialism, the nation, anti-racism, modern law and democracy bring new questions. The real task is to place these independent traditions in equal dialogue. The parallel view of Mithila draws four basic lessons from this chapter. First, the method of proof should self-review when new sources of knowledge arrive. Second—the technical discipline of tradition should not be assimilated by giving it a modern name. Third, the claims of modern institutions should be examined by the criteria of evidence and dignity. Fourth—respect for local knowledge is not a privilege free from criticism.

title: The Division between Analytic and Continental Philosophy
summary: In the history of twentieth-century philosophy, one much-discussed division emerges repeatedly—“Analytic Philosophy” and “Continental Philosophy”. At first glance, this section seems convenient, since some differences in writing styles, methodologies, institutional focuses and question choices are evident. But when this division is taken as the ultimate map of philosophical reality, then this convenience itself becomes a problem. On the one hand, the subtle problems of logic, argument, clarity, linguistic analysis, mind–language–knowledge; On the other hand, critiques of history, experience, existence, interpretation, power, culture, the body, structure, fragmentation, and modernity—this type of generalization drives students, teachers, and writers into philosophical camps instead of philosophical dialogue. Herein lies the problem with this chapter: are these divisions really names of deep philosophical oppositions, or merely convenient categories of university history? If this is partially true, then what is the limit? And what special light can the parallel traditions of India and Mithila shed on this question? The basic assertion of this chapter is that the division between analytic and continental philosophy is not entirely fabricated, but that it is basically just an acronym for historical, linguistic, institutional and methodological trends; It is not appropriate to turn it into rigid, complete, self-sufficient philosophical states. The general emphasis of the analytic tradition appears to be on clarity of argument, linguistic/conceptual analysis, formal argumentation, proximity to science and problem-focused writing. The general force of the continental tradition appears to be on the multiplicity of experience, history, interpretation, power, culture, existence, body, structure, critical socio-view and meaning. But these force lines are not without exception. Parallel philosophy therefore insists that this division be read as a useful signpost, but not as a final map of truth. The real test of philosophy is in the depth of the question, the fair presentation of the counterargument, the judgment of evidence, and self-criticism.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 3 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former argues that the clarity, rationality, and checkability of analytic philosophy are real achievements of modern philosophy. The bulk of the continental tradition shows more ambiguity, word-pollution, allegorical writing and unsubstantiated claims. Therefore, it would be a loss of rigorous philosophy to equate the two. The second form of the former comes from the opposite direction. He argues that analytic philosophy gets so caught up in excessive nuances, fragmentary problems and linguistic fragmentation that it misses the realities of history, power, colonialism, race, race, gender, the body, collective suffering, art and public life. In such a situation, the continental tradition becomes more human, more historical and more critical. The third premise argues that the association of Indian philosophy with this Western division is itself a consequence of colonial curiosity. The traditions of Nyaya, Vedanta, Mimansa, Buddhism, Jainism, Grammar, Poetics, etc. are sufficient in their independent frameworks; To read him as analytical or continental would distort the original.
uttarapaksha: The latter argues that the first warning is not negligible. Philosophy requires argument, clarity, tolerance of counterargument and conceptual discipline. But it is inconsistent to regard these qualities as the private property of only one tradition. The continental tradition also has extremely rigorous philosophical arguments; If the reader reads patiently, explores the line of reasoning, he can understand the difference between how much is vague, and how much is complex. The second caveat is also appropriate—history, power, bodies, experience, culture, memory, labor, and injustice are not the extrinsic subjects of philosophy, but its central domains. But the current development of the analytical tradition shows that it is no longer cut off from the complexities of life in ethics, political philosophy, feminist philosophy, social epistemology, philosophy of disability, race, technology, language-rights and testimony-discussion. Third, it may indeed be unfair to confine Indian philosophy to Western categories. But the comparative study itself is not flawed. The flaw is when the comparison becomes triumphalist without the evidence of history—as if “neo-justice is exactly analytic philosophy” or “emptiness is exactly deconstruction”. Parallel philosophy rejects such shortcuts.
synthesis: The division of analytic and continental philosophy is a useful hint, of course, but it is not the ultimate geography of philosophy itself. This is only a summary of historical–institutional–methodological trends. What is more decisive philosophically is how clear, how rational, how history-conscious, how aware of power relations, how self-critical and how focused on human dignity I am. Indian philosophy shows that language, logic, experience, interpretation, liberation, history, proof and plurality—all these questions can be handled in diverse forms by the same intellectual civilization. The parallel view of Mithila goes one step further and says that the subtlety of logic and the breadth of life are not contradictory. So the conclusion of parallel philosophy is clear—use this division as a study tool, but don’t make it a philosophical prison.

title: Where Does Indian Philosophy Sit on This Map?
summary: Modern university philosophy courses often appear to be framed in which the history of “Western philosophy” is presented as a continuous story from ancient Greece to modern analytical or continental flows, and “Indian philosophy” is listed in separate sections. This arrangement leads to a serious intellectual confusion—as if the general history of philosophy were the history of the West, and India a special cultural appendix to it. Because of this division, the basic questions of the Indian philosophical tradition—proof, direct, inference, word, absence, meaning, sentence, sovereign, causality, self, non-self, liberation, duty, language, logic, controversy, perception and reality—do not appear as common questions of world philosophy. On the contrary, the Indian tradition is often described as simply “spiritual” or “religious”, while Nyaya, Mimansa, Buddhist Pramanamimansa, Grammar, Jain logic, Vedanta, Lokayata and Navya-nyaya all have rigorous conceptual analysis, counter-arguments, proof-discrimination and philosophical disagreements. But the opposite of this criticism is the crisis. If, in the name of honoring Indian philosophy, it is said that all the ideas of modern analytical philosophy, linguistic philosophy, structuralism, postmodernism or philosophy of science were already available in India, history would be distorted again. Real respect comes not from antiquity-claims, but from independent question-structuring and serious study of logic. The basic assertion of this chapter is that it is inappropriate to classify Indian philosophy as either “analytic” or “continental”. Indian traditions have their own independent historical questions, methodologies, linguistic tools, textual traditions and institutional life. But his questions are not entirely separate from the general questions of world philosophy. The proper place of Indian philosophy, therefore, is not to find empty rooms within the Western map, but to make the framework of the map itself polycentric. The history of philosophy is not a line extending out from a center; There is a history of interaction between many centers, traditions, languages, scriptural debates and translations. The parallel philosophy considers India as an independent dialogue party, not an “appendix” to this polycentric map. Nyaya–neo-nyaya takes the nuances of proof and reasoning; mysticism questions of language, duty and interpretation; Buddhist philosophy critiques of non-self, transience, pratityasamutpada, emptiness and knowledge; Jain philosophy Anekant, new and conditional statements; Vedanta self–Brahman–world relationship; the challenge of popular materialism; Grammar The pervasive problem of language–sentence–meaning. Modern comparisons of these are possible, but without declaring similarities.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 4 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former can say that making Indian philosophy an “equal side” of world philosophy is an urge of modern identity politics. The criterion of philosophy is not geography or civilization, but reason; If Indian texts have world-class arguments, they should be studied, otherwise not just because of cultural pride. The other antecedent comes from the opposite direction. He says that measuring Indian philosophy by the criteria of modern world-view is itself colonialism. The Indian tradition of knowledge runs on its spiritual, instrumental and salvation-centered basis; Reading it in the modern category of logic, language or science destroys its soul. The third premise states that comparative philosophy often produces superficial similarities—e.g. “Navya-nyaya = analytic philosophy”, “Buddhist emptiness = fragmentation”, “Anekant = postmodern relativity”. Such comparisons confuse the reader. The fourth premise is that the classics of Indian philosophy are in difficult languages ​​such as Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit, etc.; Making modern comparisons through translation can destroy the original technical nuances.
uttarapaksha: The answer to the first premise is that parallel philosophy would not make geography a criterion of truth. On the contrary, they apply the same criterion to tradition—argument, proof, definition, counterargument, reference, and re-examination. Indian texts are important not because they are 'Indian', but because of their intellectual questions and arguments. Answer to the second precedent—the intimacy of tradition must be preserved, but intimacy is not immunity from criticism. The original context of the words moksha, sadhana, dharma, shastra, atma, karma etc. will be preserved; संगहि हुनकर दार्शनिक दाबी जाँचल सेहो जाएत। Reverence and criticism are not mutually exclusive, if the criticism is just. Answer to the third premise—simplified equality is indeed discarded. The parallel method would separate categories like “similar”, “dissimilar”, “partially similar”, “different historical work” and “undecided”. The value of comparison is not to prove ancestors, but to open new angles to the question. Answer to the fourth premise—original terminology is necessary for linguistic subtlety. Therefore, when translating technical terms into Maithili, the original Sanskrit/Pali/Prakrit terms will be placed in brackets where necessary, so that there is no language barrier and the meaning of the original concept is not lost. The same rule applies to modern English technical terms—main presentation in Maithili, English only as ancillary signs.
synthesis: Indian philosophy does not wait to be included in a single Western category on the map of world philosophy. It has its own history, language, questions, arguments, scriptural debates and goals. But this freedom does not mean self-exile either. Truth, knowledge, language, meaning, the self, the world, morality, liberation, justice and society—these are shared human questions. For this reason, a proper philosophical map should be multifocal. Indian traditions, analytical flows, continental flows, modern science, social theory and local knowledge—all should be brought into dialogue while preserving their historicity. The parallel traditions of Mithila provide the methodological basis for this work: antecedents, postpositions, proof, definition, linguistic subtlety, counterargument and re-examination. But this tradition itself is not without criticism. The final thread of the chapter is—placing Indian philosophy in world philosophy does not mean filling in the blanks on the Western map; It is to make the world-view map multicentric.

title: Mithila’s Parallel Point of Entry
summary: The first difficulty when bringing the philosophical tradition of Mithila into dialogue with modern world-view is that regional pride and the limits of philosophical analysis can very easily merge into each other. Mithila has been an important field of Nyaya, Navya-nyaya, Mimansa, Shastrartha, Bhashya, Panditya and multilingual intellectual culture; But this fact does not lead to the conclusion that the seeds of every stream of modern philosophy were already present in Mithila. The second difficulty comes from the opposite direction. Modern academic philosophy often treats local traditions as merely the material of history—as if the judicial or mystical thought of Mithila were merely ancient chapters of Sanskrit philosophy, with no living connection to questions of contemporary epistemology, philosophy of language, logic, philosophy of law, social philosophy or artificial intelligence. The question of this chapter is therefore not, “What did Mithila discover first?” Rather, “What are the methodological entry points in the intellectual tradition of Mithila that enable a serious, equal level of dialogue with modern and postmodern philosophy?” The basic assertion of this chapter is that the power of the parallel philosophy of Mithila lies not in a single 'great theory', but in the method of subtling the question. Mithila is not the only source of philosophy in this book, but an important methodological homeland. There are eight major points of entry to this homeland—evidence; words and sentences; lack; link; characterization and semantic expansion; definitions and boundaries; anterior–posterior; and scriptural debate–re-examination. These points of entry form interconnected, rather than separate, systems of thought. The rules of parallel philosophy are clear: Navya-nyaya should not be called a precursor to modern analytic philosophy; Mimansa should not be regarded as a copy of modern philosophy of interpretation; Scarcity-thinking should not be synonymous with modern denial-logic. Dialogue will be formed not by similarity-claims, but by careful comparison of problem-structures.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 5 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former might say that the technical language of neo-jurisprudence is so subtle and complex as to be unusable for modern readers. If simple questions cannot be answered without dozens of technical terms, then it can become an expertise barrier instead of clarity. The second former argues that the scriptural debate tradition of Mithila was mainly Sanskrit-classical, male-dominated and scholarly. Therefore, making it a model of modern democratic, vernacular or social philosophy may be an incomplete picture of history. The third premise is that subtle problems like proof, absence, relations and symptoms seem very small in the face of today's huge questions of science, technology, race, gender, the environment, democracy or artificial intelligence. The fourth premise may say that the name ‘Parallel Tradition of Mithila’ is itself a new creation; It would be inappropriate to regard it as a unbroken, uniform philosophical school from antiquity.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—technical language is a means, not a goal. Useful if the nuanced term reduces the ambiguity of the claim; If it becomes a mere display of authority, it should be abandoned. Parallel philosophy does not take every technical tool of neo-jurisprudence into modern writing; assumes its methodological discipline. Answer to the second precedent—it is imperative to acknowledge the social limitations of the classical tradition. Parallel Mithila values ​​Sanskrit scholarship, but Maithili considers folk language, women's experience, caste structure, labour, folk religion, modern education and democratic public life as equally philosophical content. Answer to the third precedent—subtlety and breadth are not mutually exclusive. Questions as vast as the ‘fairness’ of AI eventually break down into subtler questions of definition, evidence, classification, relationships, missing data and accountability. Even in democracy, caste or language policy, vague terms and wrong evidence can produce widespread injustice. Answer to the fourth precedent—The parallel tradition is not being called an unbroken ancient school. It is a modern philosophical reconstruction that takes methodological inspiration from the historical intellectual culture of Mithila. For this reason, its validity will be determined by its own logic and introspection, not by the imaginary continuation of history.
synthesis: The parallel entry point of Mithila is not a philosophical victory list. It is a list of disciplines to consider—evidence, terms, absences, relationships, characteristics, definitions, antecedents, postpositions, and scriptural arguments. This method is characterized by neither selfless imitation nor proofless egotism when communicating with modern philosophy. Neo-justice is not a modern analytic philosophy; Mimansa is not modern interpretive philosophy; But both have independent philosophical means of challenging modern questions. Mithila is not the only intellectual center in this book, but the methodological homeland. His contribution is to nuance the question, respectfully present the counterparty, examine the weight of the evidence, and leave the conclusion open to re-examination. The final formula of the chapter—the gateway to parallel philosophy is not glory, but questions; There is proof, not authority; It is not a defeat, it is a scriptural debate.

title: The Risks of Comparative Philosophy
summary: The appeal of comparative philosophy is obvious. When the same type of question, term, argument, or feeling appears in two different philosophical traditions, the reader immediately wants to make the connection. Both neo-judgment and modern analytic philosophy have linguistic subtleties; Both Buddhist apoh and modern semantic thought have questions of classification; Both Jaina polytheism and post-modern polyvisionism have a consciousness of the limitations of a single vision; Examines the relationship between experience and reality in both Advaita and some modern metaphysics. But this is where the greatest danger of comparison begins. The presence of identical questions would not prove identical principles. The same words do not prove the same concept. The same conclusion would not prove the same line of reasoning. and consideration of similar problems would not prove historical influence. If these distinctions are not made, comparative philosophy becomes a cultural pride contest instead of an inquiry into history. The second danger is West-centered comparisons. When Indian philosophical concepts are understood only by translating them into modern European or American categories—such as neo-judgment as ‘Indian analytical philosophy’, emptiness as ‘Indian fragmentation’, pluralism as ‘Indian postmodernism’— The basic assertion of this chapter is that comparative philosophy is reliable only if the comparison sets aside five levels: historical influence; problem-equality; conceptual similarity; Functional similarity; and basic variations. Combining these five levels creates confusion. To say historical influence requires contact, text, translation, quotations, travel, institutional connections or other concrete evidence. For problem-similarity, it is only enough that two traditions raise a kind of question. Conceptual similarity requires comparing definitions, arguments, limits of claims and results. Functional similarity says that two different concepts can do similar philosophical work even though they have different histories. Acknowledging basic differences is not the failure of comparative studies, but its maturity. The rule of parallel philosophy is—‘Where there is equality, so much; Differences where, apparent; effect by evidence alone.” Without this rule, comparison can turn into either self-praise or selfless imitation.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 6 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former argues that so much emphasis on history would diminish the universality of philosophy. If two ideas are logically identical, why is it necessary to prove a historical connection between them? Philosophical comparison is not effect-history, but argumentation. The second prior argues that excessive caution will render the comparison fruitless. If 'it is not at all the same', 'it is only a partial similarity' is added to each sentence, the reader will not see the obvious intellectual connection. The third antecedent asserts, in a glorious form, that ancient achievements must be exposed in order to restore the self-respect of colonized societies. Western historiography for a long time reduced the Indian contribution; Therefore, the ‘used to be’ claim is a countervailing correction. The fourth premise states that it is difficult to explain ancient ideas without modern philosophical language. The reader would not understand ‘deductiveness’ or ‘apoh’, but might understand ‘analysis’ or ‘fragmentation’; Therefore, modern comparison is a useful approach to teaching.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—it is not necessary for philosophical comparison to prove historical influence; But if an effect is claimed, proof is indispensable. Logical similarity is independently valuable. The problem lies where rational similarity is to be taken as a relation of history. Answer to the second precedent—caution does not mean ambiguity. On the contrary, the five-level method gives the reader more explicit language: ‘problem-similarity strong’, ‘conceptual similarity limited’, ‘no evidence of historical impact’, ‘functional similarity notable’. This language is more useful than the simple dichotomy of ‘same’/‘dissimilar’. Answer to the third premise—historical injustices will not be corrected by new historical exaggerations. The best basis for self-esteem is proven achievement. The real achievements of Mithila, India or any other tradition are so rich that there is no need to add imaginary precedents. Answer to the fourth premise—modern comparison may be an aid to teaching, but auxiliary analogies should be explicitly called ‘analogies’. Basic terms, basic questions and historical context should be gradually taught to the reader; The meaning of the concept should not be changed in the name of convenience.
synthesis: The purpose of comparative philosophy is not only to find similarities; There is also looking at the appropriate variation. Two traditions may share a question, but have different concepts, different evidence and different goals. Parallel philosophy therefore sets aside five levels—historical influence, problem-similarity, conceptual similarity, functional similarity, basic differences. This distinction makes the comparison more truthful. The tradition of Mithila is respected not by proving it to be the precursor of modern Western thought, but by reading the subtleties of its own logic, evidence, language, arguments, answers and scriptural debates. The final formula of the chapter is—compare, but do not fabricate history; Look for similarities, but don’t erase differences; Communicate, but do not copy one tradition to another.

title: Frege: Logic, Meaning and Reference
part: Analytic Philosophy and the New World of Logic
summary: In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, philosophy faced a serious question—how to express logic in a more rigorous form, apart from psychological habits, linguistic grammar, or traditional term logic? Questions of mathematical proofs, numbers, universal statements, relations and identities crossed the boundaries of ordinary grammar. Gottlob Frege tried in this crisis to develop a language of reasoning in which the logical form of the statement is more explicit. But Frege's importance is not limited to formal logic. His work opens up a basic problem in the philosophy of language: Why might two different expressions refer to the same thing, yet have different intellectual value to knowing them? Both ‘morning star’ and ‘evening star’ refer to the planet Venus, but knowing ‘morning star = evening star’ is not as trivial as ‘morning star = morning star’. This problem illustrates two dimensions of meaning. To what object or truth-value an expression points—this is its reference; The way in which the object is presented to me—it is its sense. The basic assertion of this chapter is that Frege is a crucial turning point in modern analytic philosophy, since his work brought about changes on three levels: the formalization of logic; attempts to separate meaning from psychological feeling; and distinctions between contexts and modes of presentation of linguistic expression. For Frege, logic is not just a description of how humans actually think, but a normative discipline of how to draw the right conclusions. For this reason, logic cannot merge with psychology. His basic teaching in the philosophy of language is that meaning would not be complete by simply asking ‘what object?’. ‘In what manner was that object presented?’ must also be asked. The same context may be expressed by a different sense.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 7 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former might say that the distinction between semantics and context is highly abstract. A person speaking an ordinary language would not think of 'mode of presentation' and 'context' separately; To what extent, then, do these philosophical distinctions represent actual linguistic practice? The second premise says that it is unnatural to treat the context of a sentence as a truth-value. A sentence is about an event, situation, or fact; To call ‘true’ or ‘false’ its context can seem like imposing a framework of formal logic on language. The third premise is on the concept–object distinction. In natural language, terms like 'humanity', 'redness' or 'truth' take on object-like noun forms. If concepts are not logically objects, then why does language seem to repeatedly break this category distinction? The fourth premise is from the Indian perspective. The Indian tradition has lengthy discussions on word–meaning, syntax, characteristics, caste, person, absence, relationship and proof; In such a case, it would be Eurocentric history to call Frege the ‘beginning of the philosophy of language’.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—the philosophical distinction is used here not to be a direct imitation of practice, but to clarify epistemic differences. A normal speaker may not use the word 'meaningful', however, he understands that 'morning star' and 'evening star' convey different information. The theory formalizes this distinction. The answer to the second precedent—taking the truth-value of a sentence as a referent—should be understood within Frege’s broader logical project. It is not a simple definition of normal linguistic feeling, but a proposition designed for the logical explanation of joint statements and substitutions. Answer to the third premise—the concept–object distinction indeed creates tension with natural language; This tension was experienced by Frege himself. For this reason, his theory is not exempt from criticism. But category distinctions remain a powerful means of clarifying logical roles. Answer to the fourth premise—Frege is not the universal beginning of the philosophy of language, but the decisive turning point of the modern European analytic tradition. There is already a history of independent linguistic philosophies of the Nyaya, Mimansa, Grammar, Buddhist and Jain traditions. Parallel philosophy acknowledges this polycentric history.
synthesis: Frege is decisive in the history of modern analytic philosophy because his work gave a new formal rigor to questions of logic, mathematics, and the philosophy of language. The distinction between semantic perception and context makes it clear that object designation is not merely the entirety of meaning. The same object can be known by a different mode of presentation, and this difference produces new knowledge. Frege's ideas about concept–object, function–logic, context–theory and truth–value are powerful, but do not encompass all the dimensions of ordinary language. Later philosophies of language will expand this boundary. Indian jurisprudence, mysticism, grammar and Buddhist semantics are independent intellectual traditions. The neo-justice of Mithila is not a precursor to Frege; But the dialogue about linguistic clarity, relationship analysis and the limits of claims is very fruitful.

title: Russell: Description, Logical Form and the World
part: Analytic Philosophy and the New World of Logic
summary: One of the basic questions of Bertrand Russell's philosophy of language is whether ordinary sentences always have the same actual logical structure as they sound. Language too often presents grammatical forms as if the sentences were the names of a specific object, while logical analysis shows that those expressions actually make complex claims to existence, unity, and attributions. The classic example is—‘the current king of France is bald.’ On the surface of the sentence, ‘the current king of France’ sounds like a noun, as if something is already available and is being given the ‘bald’ quality. But when France does not have a current king, the question arises: is the sentence meaningless, untrue, or about something imaginary? Russell's definitive description theory solves this difficulty by logical analysis. He shows that ‘the present king of France’ is in fact not a name, but a brief descriptive structure: there is a single person who is the present French king; Such a person is the only one; And he is bald. The basic assertion of this chapter is that Russell’s theory of description is a powerful example of ‘analysis’ in philosophy. Rewriting complex or confusing grammatical sentences into more explicit logical forms can reduce unnecessary metaphysical claims about existence, unity, properties and context. For Russell, definitive descriptions—such as ‘so-and-so’s only king’, ‘author of this book’, ‘the greatest prime number’—are not the same as generic names. They are expressions of imperfect signs; His meaning unfolds in the logical structure of the whole sentence. An important consequence of description theory is that the need to assume names for non-existent objects decreases. Instead of assuming a strange fantasy entitled ‘the present king of France’, the sentence can be analyzed as an existential claim, and that claim can turn out to be untrue.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 8 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former might say that Russell's analysis unnecessarily formalizes ordinary language. Normal speakers would not think in the form ‘existence + unity + quality’; The theory may then be merely a philosophical rewriting instead of a real meaning. The second precedent states, like the famous Disha after Strawson, that in uttering a sentence like ‘the present king of France is bald’ the speaker does not necessarily ‘say’ the existence of the king, but rather presupposes it. If the presupposition fails, a simple untruthfulness of the sentence would not capture the nuances of linguistic behavior. The third premise suggests that Russell's search for logical forms can produce a latent idealism in philosophy—as if the language of formal logic were more real than natural language. The fourth premise is from the Indian perspective. The complex discussion of syntax, characteristics, absence, relationship, caste–person and word proof is very old in the Nyaya–Mimansa tradition; Then, while acknowledging the importance of description theory, it is not appropriate to consider it as a universal linguistic solution.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—Russell's aim is not to mimic the psychological processes of normal speakers, but to elucidate the logical structure of the truth-condition of a sentence. Analysis is useful when it reduces philosophical difficulty, rather than describing every nuance of colloquialism. The criticism regarding the answer—presupposition of the second precedent is important. In ordinary language, the distinction between statements, presuppositions, signs and contexts is more complex than Russell's original theory. Parallel philosophy sees this criticism not as Russell's defeat, but as the next development of the philosophy of language. Answer to the third premise—formal language is a means of analysis, not a competitor of natural language. Useful when formalism reduces confusion; When they erase context, behavior or social meaning, limitations must be acknowledged. Answer to the fourth premise—the freedom of Indian language and philosophy is fully acceptable. Russell's theory of description should not be declared a precursor or successor to judicial or mystical theory. Questions and dialogue will be limited and explicit.
synthesis: Russell’s theory of description is an ideal example of modern analytic philosophy—finding logical structure beneath the surface of linguistic form. Analyzing definite descriptions as combined claims of existence, unity, and quality, rather than as names, reduces many confusions about non-existent things. Russell's project sheds serious light on the relationship between language and the world, but without encompassing the whole of the context, presuppositions, speaker-intentions and social usage of ordinary language. The latter philosophy of language develops from this boundary. Indian Nyaya–Mimansa–Buddhist discussions and the Navya-nyaya of Mithila offer an independent solution to this question. Parallel philosophy seeks problem-dialogue, not similarity.

title: Moore and Common Sense
part: Analytic Philosophy and the New World of Logic
summary: One of the old powers of philosophical skepticism is that it can call into question nearly all the certainties of ordinary life. Do I really have knowledge of the external world? Do I know for certain the existence of my hands, the table, the house, other human beings or my own body? Is it not possible that my experience is the result of a deception, a dream or some widespread delusion? G.S. E. Moore adopts a distinctive philosophical strategy in the face of this crisis. He does not give the skeptic the right to assume that firm knowledge of ordinary life is automatically canceled because of philosophical principles. His insistence is—I know some general facts, such as ‘this is my hand’, ‘the earth existed even before I was born’, ‘there are other human beings’, ‘I have a body’—with more certainty than philosophical skeptical arguments. The question of this approach is not simply ‘is common sense correct’. The more profound question is: When philosophical theory and firm common sense collide, who has the burden of proof? Is common sense automatically the ultimate criterion of knowledge? Are they merely incipient beliefs, which should undergo philosophical scrutiny? The basic assertion of this chapter is that the power of Moore's philosophy lies not in its blind endorsement of 'common sense', but in its reversal of the burden of proof of philosophical argument. If a philosophical theory comes to the conclusion that ‘I do not know the existence of my own hands’, Moore asks—is that theory really more certain than this common sense? Moore would not consider common-sense to be an instinctive response devoid of reason. He considers some pre-theoretical epistemological claims so strong that philosophical theories must provide very strong evidence to succeed against them. The famous display of the external world—one hand showing ‘here is one hand’, the other hand showing ‘here is the other hand’—is a dramatization of this request. Moore's aim is not to provide a psychological solution to all skepticism, but to show that I have some direct knowledge of the existence of external objects.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 9 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former states that common-sense changes culturally, historically, and socially. Sometimes society considered slavery, caste hierarchy, female inequality or superstition as ‘normal’. It can be dangerous, then, to make common-sense a philosophical criterion. The other precedent is skeptical. He says—Moore assumes 'this is the hand' and admits the same thing he had to prove first. If the possibility of dreams or delusions is in question, showing hands does not solve the problem. The third presupposition says that the question of the existence of the external world is a linguistic or metaphysical one, not merely an empirical demonstration. The basis of the public identity of the ‘hand’ may itself rely on the principle of relation to the world. The fourth antecedent is in morality. The mere possibility of an ‘open question’ does not prove that ‘good’ is not essentially identical with a natural quality. Language-wise, the question may remain open, although reality-wise, there is identity.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—parallel philosophy does not treat common sense as the same as every belief in social tradition. Direct facts of the ‘this is the hand’ type and social ideas of the ‘such and such race is superior’ type do not belong to the same category. The philosophical value of common sense should be examined according to the type of claim. The answer to the second precedent—Moore would not have forbidden the possibility of skepticism; He brings into question the relative certainty of the evidence. If ‘this is the hand’ knowledge is stronger than the skeptical hypothesis, then direct knowledge will not be canceled on the basis of possible confusion alone. Answer to the third premise—language and metaphysics are of course important; But it would be equally excessive to regard direct experience as merely the product of theory. Public objects—knowledge, action, touch, sight, and the affirmations of other individuals—form a solid basis for relations with the world. The answer to the fourth premise—the open-question argument—was subjected to numerous subsequent criticisms. The parallel view sees this as a means of conceptual caution, not ultimate moral proof: factual properties and moral values ​​should not be assumed to be the same without additional argument.
synthesis: G.S. E. Moore's common-sense philosophy is a philosophical resistance against radical skepticism. His main force is the question—what do I know more certainly: the existence of my own hands, or philosophical arguments that say I don’t know my own hands? Evidence of the external world, common-sense certainty, and moral ‘open questions’—in all three places Moore teaches caution against conceptual excess. But common sense is not infallible. Science improves it; Social criticism challenges him; Confusion shows its limits. Therefore, parallel philosophy would not have turned Moore into blind generalism. The dialogue between judicial realism and Moore is particularly fruitful, since both acknowledge the external world and the possibility of direct knowledge. But the judgment provides a more elaborate evidentiary structure, and the Indian counterpart constantly checks this realism.

title: Early Wittgenstein: Language, Fact, Picture and the Limits of Expression
part: Analytic Philosophy and the New World of Logic
summary: Central to the philosophical project of early Ludwig Wittgenstein is a hard question—how does language make meaningful statements about the world? If a sentence is true or false about reality, what structural relationship exists between the sentence and the world that makes meaning possible? Against the backdrop of this question is the logical revolution of Frege and Russell. The superficial grammar of a normal language too often hides the real logical structure. The early Wittgenstein gives this idea a more comprehensive form: a meaningful statement is a logical picture of the possible state of the world. But that is not the only problem. If language can only depict factual situations, how far is morality, beauty, the meaning of life, God, values ​​or philosophy itself narrative? This is where early Wittgenstein’s famous idea of ​​limits comes in—some things cannot be ‘said’ in language, although they can be ‘seen’. The basic assertion of this chapter is that the early Wittgenstein offers a structural paradigm of philosophy of language: the world is not merely a collection of things, but a composite of facts; The sentence is a picture of possible facts; Pictures and facts should share a logical form; And the limits of meaningful statements are linked to this capacity for depiction. The task of philosophy in this project is not to discover new facts, but to clarify the logical limits of thought and language. Philosophy becomes an act of explanation instead of a collection of theories. The early Wittgenstein distinguishes between ‘what can be said’ and ‘what only appears’. The logical form itself would not be described fact-like by the sentence; it manifests itself in linguistic semantic structures.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 10 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former argues that the ‘sentence = picture’ theory restricts language too much. Questions, commands, prayers, words, jokes, metaphors, poems, satire, legal declarations and social expressions are not just facts. The second premise says that ‘logical form’ is a highly abstract concept. If it cannot be said directly, how clear is its philosophical use? This theory itself may seem to rely on unprovable structures. The third premise is ethical. If a moral sentence is not a factual statement, should 'murder is wrong' or 'injustice is unjust' be meaningless? Such a conclusion may seem unacceptable to moral philosophy. The fourth premise is from the Indian perspective. The Upanishads, Buddhism, Vedanta, Mimansa and philosophy of language have lengthy discussions of narrativity, ineffability, the limits of words and the ultimate truth. To regard early Wittgenstein’s thought of limits as a uniquely universal quest, then, reduces the polycentricity of history.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—picture theory is primarily a project to understand the logical structure of declarative statements. Its full goal is not to cover all the functions of a common language. This limitation itself accounts for the transformation of later Wittgenstein's philosophy. Answer to the second premise—the idea of ​​logical forms ‘looking’ is difficult, of course, but the purpose is to point out that it is not appropriate to make the condition of representation another object of the facts represented. This is the humility of metaphysics. Answer to the third premise—parallel philosophy would not have accepted early Wittgenstein’s factual theory of meaning as the ultimate criterion for moral truth. The justification of moral statements can be checked by public reason, human dignity, experience, consequences, rights and reason. The answer to the fourth precedent—a comparison with the Indian ineffability discussion—is possible, but with caution. ‘Neti-neti’, emptiness, non-alternativeness, the ineffability or wordlimit of Brahman have their own historical projects; He should not be declared to be identical with the early Wittgensteinian theory of logical limits.
synthesis: The early Wittgensteinian philosophy is an ambitious attempt to understand the relationship between language and the world in structural terms. The world is the set of facts, the sentence is the picture of possible facts, and the logical form is the condition of the depiction. In this view, truth and meaningfulness are separate questions: untrue sentences can also be meaningful if they depict possible facts. Philosophically, his most profound teaching is perhaps boundary-judgment—call the obvious what can be said to be logically obvious; Do not fill with metaphysical speculations about which language creates confusion. But a parallel philosophy would not make this principle of limitation a prohibition of moral, religious, aesthetic, or social experience. Different types of claims may have different justifications.

title: Logical Positivism: Verification, Science and the Limits of Metaphysics
part: Analytic Philosophy and the New World of Logic
summary: In the first half of the twentieth century, some philosophers and scientific thinkers faced an acute question—what is the criterion for the meaning of a philosophical statement? Statements of science are associated with experiments, observations, calculations and public scrutiny; But the statements of many metaphysicians seemed to be neither verifiable nor refutable, yet they claimed serious knowledge. Thinkers such as Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Karnap, Otto Neurath, Hans Hahn and others belonging to the Vienna Circle tried to solve this crisis by the combined criteria of logic, modern science and experience. This pervasive trend is often referred to as ‘logical directism’ or ‘logical empiricism’. The original assertion was that two major types of meaningful statements can be identified: one, analytical statements of logic and mathematics; Second, factual statements that can be checked by experience. Many metaphysical statements that fell outside this criterion were regarded as dubious as epistemological claims. The basic assertion of this chapter is that logical directivism was an essential intellectual purification effort in modern philosophy. He wanted to make philosophical language responsive to proof, reason, science, and public scrutiny. But logical directism was no longer a rigid, uniform doctrine. Strong forms of verification quickly ran into difficulty; Later, views on confirmation, testability, observation statements, theory language, and the unity of science changed. Parallel philosophy draws three lessons from this tradition—skepticism of unsubstantiated vast claims; linguistic clarity; and public scrutiny. But he would not regard single ‘empirical verification’ as the sole criterion for all domains of knowledge.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 11 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the precedent states that the verification principle is too narrow. Many meaningful sentences of human life—morality, beauty, history, law, love, memory, religious experience—would not be laboratory-verified. The second precedent is from the philosophy of science. The observation itself is not free of principle; What was observed, which instruments are reliable, which data are significant—all are influenced by prior knowledge and theory. The third premise says that without metaphysics, science itself assumes certain beliefs—the stability of reality, causality, the external world, mathematical structure, regularity. Therefore, it may be self-contradictory to say that all metaphysics is 'meaningless' The fourth premise is from the Indian perspective. Nyaya, Mimansa, Buddhist and Jain philosophies give a complex assortment of proofs; Direct is not the only source of knowledge. Words, inferences, metaphors, memory, absence, etc. raise different questions. The directivist criterion, then, seems historically highly unilinear.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—the best teaching of logical directivism is not in the sense that ‘where there is no laboratory, there is no meaning’. The proper teaching is that each knowledge claim should make its justification clear. The answer to the second precedent—observations may be theory-relative, but this would not make the facts entirely arbitrary. Errors can be reduced by tools, repetition, independent testing, interdisciplinary review and public statistics. The answer to the third precedent—not all questions of metaphysics are the same. Some claims may be precursors to genuine scientific or logical questions; some conceptual clarification; Some may actually be languages ​​that survive testing. Parallel philosophy does not reject metaphysics in one fell swoop, but examines it claim by claim. Answer to the fourth premise—the plurality of Indian proof traditions offers a constructive extension, not just a critique of directism. Different types of evidence can be assumed for different areas, but the reliability, limitations and error-conditions of each evidence should be clear.
synthesis: Logical Probability was the most powerful movement of proof, logic, science, and linguistic clarity in the history of modern philosophy. His goal was to free philosophy from vague metaphysical claims and make it liable to public scrutiny. But rigorous verification-theory itself ran into difficulties concerning scientific laws, theoretical objects, history, ethics, and its own semantic criterion. This caused logical empiricism to become more subtle over time. The Indian evidence tradition shows that the sources of knowledge can be multiple. Mithila's parallel vision connects this plurality to modern scrutiny, public reason and self-criticism. Hence the formula of the parallel philosophy is—ask for proof, but do not close the proof in one kind; Check metaphysics, but do not call it meaningless by name; Respect science, but do not adopt scientism.

title: Carnap and the Question of Metaphysics
part: Analytic Philosophy and the New World of Logic
summary: At the heart of Rudolf Carnap’s philosophy is a hard question—when does philosophical language make genuine epistemological claims, and when does it become a pseudo-sentence that appears meaningful only because of its grammatical form? In the broader project of logical directivism, Carnap sharpened this question through logical analysis, science-language, and symbolic syntax. The target of Carnap's initial criticism was metaphysical statements that sound serious, but when examined for their semantics, syntax, truth-conditions, or testability, would not yield clear factual claims. In his view, many traditional metaphysical controversies may in fact arise from linguistic confusion, category errors, or ambiguities in the rules of expression. But the problem does not end here. If metaphysics is just a meaningless linguistic relic, what is the status of questions like ‘numbers exist’, ‘physical objects are real’, ‘scientific theories describe the external world’, ‘potential is a real quality’? Science itself uses concepts that would not be found in direct experience. The basic assertion of this chapter is that Carnap's philosophical contribution is more subtle than a simple prohibition of metaphysics. His main strength is the insistence that the linguistic form, logical categories, truth-conditions and methods of testing of philosophical statements be made explicit. In Carnap's early view, many metaphysical statements may be 'pseudo-sentences'—that is, they have a grammatical form, but the logical form or testable meaning is not clear. At a later stage, he acknowledges more the importance of a plurality of linguistic frameworks and practical choices. The ‘principle of tolerance’ is the central thread of this development: a single philosophical language is not absolutely essential; Different formal linguistic systems can be created for different purposes, provided the rules are clear.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 12 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former argues that Carnap reduces serious questions of metaphysics to rules of language. The question ‘What is the world really?’ cannot simply be a ‘Which language is convenient?’ question. The second premise suggests that adopting a linguistic framework is not a neutral pragmatic choice at all. What is valid, what evidence is admissible, what classification is useful—these are linked to social, scientific, and sometimes political values. The third antecedent is from the direction of Quine. The rigid distinction between ‘analytic’ and ‘synthetic’ statements, the clear boundaries of linguistic rules and empirical facts—these can themselves be problematic. If the whole web of language and belief collides with experience, then the Carnapean level-distinction would not be so clear. The fourth premise is from the Indian perspective. Nyaya presents metaphysical categories such as matter, quality, action, general, special, combination, absence, etc., not merely as linguistic conveniences, but as claims about the actual structure of the world. It would be a misreading of judicial realism to call such a claim merely a framework-selection.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—Carnap's criticism would not automatically destroy every question of metaphysics. His strongest insistence is that questions such as ‘What is the world really?’ should be clarified in such a way that the distinction of answers, the possibilities of proof and the use of concepts can be recognized. Answer to the second precedent—framework selection cannot truly be value-neutral. Parallel philosophy extends Carnap on this point: along with simplicity and fruitfulness, justice, access, transparency, historical impact and human dignity can also be framework-evaluation criteria. Answer to the third precedent—Quine’s critique reconstitutes Carnap’s project, not eliminates it. Even if the relationship between language and experience is considered more complex, conceptual clarity, rule analysis and claim-type distinctions remain useful. Answer to the fourth premise—Judicial metaphysics should not be called merely a linguistic framework. The parallel method will read the judgment with its own realistic claims, proofs, and counterarguments; The Carnapian analysis will only ask what the meaning, weight of proof and logical limits of this claim are.
synthesis: Karnapa's philosophy is a deeper language-criticism than a simple prohibition of metaphysics. He insists that the terms, categories, rules, logical forms, and tests of philosophical statements be clear. The development of Carnap from the early ‘pseudo-sentence’ critique to the later ‘linguistic framework’, ‘internal–external questions’ and ‘theory of tolerance’ admits of greater plurality in philosophy. But a parallel philosophy would not make framework-plurality moral or realistic arbitrariness. Frameworks can be checked on criteria of evidence, usefulness, clarity, social consequences and dignity. The Indian Nyaya, Buddhist, Mimansa and Jain traditions have an independent history of Tattva Mimansa. Carnap not his former judge; His language discrimination is a means of comparative examination.

title: Quine: The Crisis of the Analytic–Synthetic Distinction
part: Analytic Philosophy and the New World of Logic
summary: A basic premise of modern empiricism was the distinction that some statements are ‘analytic’—that is, true only because of semantics, definitions, or logical laws—and others are ‘synthetic’—that is, true or false because of facts about the world. ‘All bachelors are unmarried’, for example, seems analytical; ‘There are four chairs in this room’ is an empirical synthetic statement. W. W. McCarthy. V.O. Quine puts this easy distinction in serious trouble. His famous critique asks—on what basis should ‘analytic’ statements really be identified? If so, because of ‘synonymy’, how should synonymity itself be defined? If because of ‘definition’, then on what basis does the definition add synonyms? If because of ‘necessary truth’, how is necessity to be explained apart from analyticity itself? Quine’s second goal is ‘reductionism’—the idea that every meaningful statement can ultimately be linked to a separate set of direct experiences. In his view, knowledge confronts experience not as separate sentences, but as interconnected belief-networks. The basic assertion of this chapter is that Quine restructures modern empiricism from the inside. He would not deny the importance of the experience; On the contrary, he argues that the relationship of language and theory to experience is not simple as a sentence–an experience. The critique of the analytic–synthetic distinction is based on the claim that the interdependent concepts of synonymy, definition, necessity, and linguistic rules can form a circle without independent interpretation. Quine's confirmation holism says that the whole belief-net comes up to the test of experience. At any one inspection-contradiction, we can modify supporting beliefs, calculations, tools, definitions or central principles—anything.
source: Gajendra Thakur’s Parallel Philosophy, Volume II · supplied Maithili Chapter 13 · English translation
purvapaksha: The first form of the former states that there is a clear difference between ‘all bachelors are unmarried’ and ‘all bachelors are six feet tall’. If Quine could not adequately philosophize this difference, then his critique seems to run counter to general linguistic facts. The second presupposition says that linguistic rules themselves can be the basis of analytic truth. Learning a language means accepting certain usage rules; Because of this rule, some sentences are true. The third premise is on the whole. If any part of the theory can be saved in the face of any experience, then science can be arbitrary. Where is the real power of scientific refutation left? The fourth premise is from the Indian perspective. The Nyaya, Mimansa and Grammar traditions subtly distinguish between semantics, definition, syntax and proof. Such broad totalities as ‘all meanings are in networks of relations’ can blur the local distinctions of this tradition.
uttarapaksha: Answer to the first premise—Quine would not deny the existence of linguistic differences; What, he asks, is the basis for philosophically regarding this difference as such a rigid limit that some sentences become entirely independent of experience? Answer to the second premise—linguistic rules can provide useful explanations, but the rules themselves can be changed by historical language practices, institutional traditions, and scientific purposes. Therefore, ‘rules’ are not entirely world-averse foundations. Answer to the third precedent—totality is not arbitrary. The scientific community chooses revisions by criteria such as simplicity, predictability, comprehensiveness, consistency with prior knowledge, repeatability of experiments, and independent evidence. Not all parts of the network are replaceable at the same cost. Answer to the fourth premise—the subtle differences of Indian tradition are not a challenge to the whole, but an improvement. Parallel philosophy assumes a multi-level network in which direct, inferential, word, definition, behavior, memory and social evidence function separately.
synthesis: Quine’s ‘two principles of empiricism’ raise serious questions about the analytic–synthetic distinction and the foundations of rigorous reductionism. His main teaching is not that there is no distinction between language, reason, and experience; Rather, it is difficult to consider these distinctions as self-evident, completely independent foundations. The totality of belief-networks views knowledge in terms of the interrelations of context, supporting beliefs, and principles. Experience exerts pressure on the net, but in what part the modification will take place—it is a question of broad discretion. Indian Pramanamimansa and the Navya-nyaya of Mithila give local nuanced analysis; Quine Wide Web consciousness. The parallel philosophy combines the two to develop a multilevel, error-correctable evidentiary discrimination.

title: Analytic Philosophy and Navya-Nyāya
part: Analytic Philosophy and the New World of Logic
summary: In modern comparative philosophy, the comparison between neo-jurisprudence and analytic philosophy is very fascinating.
